## Length Chasing and Incircles

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Ratios of directed lengths are treated as ratios of vectors along the same line.
:::

::: {#thm-2point1}
## Menelaus's Theorem
Let $D,E,F$ lie on $BC,AC,AB$, respectively. Then
$$
\frac{BD}{DC}\times\frac{CE}{EA}\times\frac{AF}{FB}=-1
$$
if and only if $D,E,F$ are collinear (where lengths are directed).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
In three-dimensional space, choose points $P,Q,R$ such that $PA,QB,RC$ are perpendicular to plane $ABC$.

Since the product of ratios is $-1$, we can choose the signed distances of $P,Q,R$ from plane $ABC$ so that the triples $(Q,D,R)$, $(R,E,P)$, and $(P,F,Q)$ are each collinear.

Hence plane $PQR$ intersects plane $ABC$ along the line through $D,E,F$, so $D,E,F$ are collinear.
:::

::: {#thm-2point2}
## Ceva's Theorem
Let $D,E,F$ lie on $BC,AC,AB$, respectively. Then
$$
\frac{BD}{DC}\times\frac{CE}{EA}\times\frac{AF}{FB}=1
$$
if and only if $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent (where lengths are directed).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let the three lines concur at $P$. The ratios of directed segments correspond to ratios of signed areas of $\triangle BCP$, $\triangle CAP$, and $\triangle ABP$, whose product is clearly $1$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Two triangles $A_1B_1C_1$ and $A_2B_2C_2$ are **perspective** if $A_1A_2, B_1B_2, C_1C_2$ are concurrent; their point of concurrency is called the **perspector** (or **center of perspectivity**).
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The **cevian triangle** of a point $X$ is the triangle with vertices $AX\cap BC$, $BX\cap CA$, and $CX\cap AB$, and the **cevian circle** of $X$ is the circumcircle of these three points.
:::

::: {#lem-2point1}
Let $D,E,F$ lie on $BC,AC,AB$, respectively, such that $\triangle DEF$ and $\triangle ABC$ are perspective. Then $BC\cap EF$, $CA\cap FD$, and $AB\cap DE$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows by length chasing using @thm-2point1 and @thm-2point2.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
If the perspector in @lem-2point1 is $P$ and the line of collinearity is $\ell$, then $\ell$ is called the **trilinear polar** of $P$, and $P$ is called the **trilinear pole** of $\ell$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point2}
The trilinear polar of $H$ is perpendicular to the Euler line.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Considering the radical center of $(ABC)$, the nine-point circle, and $(BC)$ shows that the radical axis of $(ABC)$ and the nine-point circle is precisely the trilinear polar of $H$.
:::

::: {#thm-2point3}
## Monge's Theorem
The exsimilicenter of three circles taken pairwise are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Take the triangle formed by the three centers as the reference triangle; the result follows from the ratio of radii and @thm-2point1.
:::

::: {#thm-2point4}
The reference triangle and its contact triangle are perspective.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows immediately by length chasing and @thm-2point2.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The perspector of the reference triangle and its contact triangle is the **Gergonne point** $X(7)$, denoted by $Ge$ unless otherwise stated.
:::

::: {#thm-2point5}
Let $DEF$ be the cevian triangle of $X$, and let $D',E',F'$ be the reflections of $D,E,F$ across $M_{BC},M_{CA},M_{AB}$, respectively. Then $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle D'E'F'$ are perspective.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This follows immediately by length chasing and @thm-2point2.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The perspector in @thm-2point5 is called the **isotomic conjugate** of $X$.
:::

::: {#cor-2point1}
The isotomic conjugate of $G$ is $G$ itself.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The isotomic conjugate of $Ge$ is the **Nagel point** $X(8)$, denoted by $Na$ unless otherwise stated.
:::

::: {#lem-2point3}
If the incircle and the $A$-excircle touch $BC$ at $D$ and $T$, respectively, then $M_{BC}=M_{DT}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By length chasing, $BT=CD$.
:::

::: {#cor-2point2}
$A$, $Na$, and the point of tangency of the $A$-excircle with $BC$ are collinear.
:::

::: {#lem-2point4}
Let the incircle and the $A$-excircle of $\triangle ABC$ touch $BC$ at $D$ and $T$, respectively, and let $D'$ be the reflection of $D$ across $I$. Then $A,D',T$ are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Note that $A$ is the exsimilicenter of the incircle and the $A$-excircle.

Moreover, $D'$ and $T$ are corresponding points under this homothety (their tangents to the two circles are both parallel to $BC$).

Hence $D'T$ passes through the exsimilicenter $A$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point5}
If the $A$-excircle touches $BC$ at $T$, then $TI$ passes through the midpoint of the $A$-altitude.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $A_{\perp BC}=F$ and $M_{AF}=N$, and keep the notation of @lem-2point4.

The homothety centered at $T$ sending $D$ and $D'$ to $F$ and $A$ maps $I$ (the midpoint of $DD'$) to $N$ (the midpoint of $FA$).
:::

::: {#cor-2point3}
Using the notation of @lem-2point4 and @lem-2point5, if $T'$ is the reflection of $T$ across $I_A$, then $A,D,T'$ are collinear, and $D,I_A,N$ are collinear.
:::

::: {#lem-2point6}
Let $I_A'$ be the reflection of $I_A$ across $BC$. Then $I_A'I$ passes through the foot of the $A$-altitude.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Keep the notation of @lem-2point4 and @lem-2point5.

By @lem-2point4, the homothety centered at $I$ sending $A$ and $N$ to $I_A$ and $T$ maps $F$ to $I_A'$.
:::

::: {#cor-2point4}
If $A_{\perp BC}=F$, then $BC$ bisects $\angle IFI_A$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point7}
The anticomplement of $I$ is $Na$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Keep the notation of @lem-2point4 and @lem-2point5.

By @lem-2point3, applying a homothety centered at $D$ with ratio $2$ maps $IM_{BC}$ to $D'T$.

By @lem-2point4, $A,Na,D',T$ are collinear and $D'T\parallel M_{BC}I$, which yields the result.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The radical center of the three excircles is $X(10)$ (the **Spieker center**), denoted by $Sp$ unless otherwise stated.
:::

::: {#lem-2point8}
The complement of $I$ is $Sp$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
The radical axis of the $B$-excircle $(I_B)$ and the $C$-excircle $(I_C)$ passes through $M_{BC}$ and is parallel to $AI$; hence $Sp$ is the incenter of the medial triangle.
:::

::: {#cor-2point5}
$I,G,Na,Sp$ are collinear, and the midpoint of $INa$ is $Sp$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point9}
Let $AI$ intersect $BC$ and $(ABC)$ at $P$ and $M$, respectively. Then $MB^2=MC^2=MP\cdot MA$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By angle chasing, $(BAP)$ is tangent to $BA$, from which the result follows.
:::

::: {#cor-2point6}
Let $A,B,M$ lie on a circle $\omega$ with $AM=BM$. If $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on $\omega$ and $MP,MQ$ intersect $AB$ at $P',Q'$, respectively, then $P,Q,P',Q'$ are concyclic.
:::

::: {#lem-2point10}
Let the incircle touch $BC$ at $D$, and let $AI$ intersect $(ABC)$ again at $M$. Then $MD$, $(AI)$, and $(ABC)$ are concurrent.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $MD$ intersect $(ABC)$ again at $X$. By @lem-1point3 and @lem-2point9, we have $MI^2=MX\cdot MD$.

Thus $(IXD)$ is tangent to $MI$. Letting $N$ be the antipode of $M$ on $(ABC)$, we have
$$
\measuredangle AXI=\measuredangle MIX+\measuredangle XAM=\measuredangle IDM+\measuredangle XNM=\measuredangle NMX+\measuredangle XNM=90^\circ.
$$
:::

::: {#cor-2point7}
Let $T$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $I_A$ to $BC$, and let $AI$ intersect $(ABC)$ again at $M$. Then $MT$, $(ABC)$, and $(AI_A)$ are concurrent.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
$X(56)$ and $X(55)$ are the exsimilicenter and insimilicenter of the circumcircle and the incircle, respectively; both lie on $OI$.
:::

::: {#cor-2point8}
Using the notation of @lem-2point10, $X(56),M,D,X$ are collinear.
:::

::: {#lem-2point11}
$(AI)$ is tangent to $(IBC)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-1point3, the line of centers passes through the intersection point $I$ and is perpendicular to the common internal tangent (the external angle bisector at $I$), so the two circles are tangent at $I$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point12}
Let $S$ lie on $(ABC)$ such that $AS\perp SI$, and let $AS\cap BC=X$. Then $XI\perp IA$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the radical center $X$ of $(AI)$, $(IBC)$, and $(ABC)$.

By @lem-2point11, the common tangent to $(AI)$ and $(IBC)$ at $I$ passes through $X$ and is perpendicular to $AI$.
:::

::: {#cor-2point9}
Let $S'$ lie on $(ABC)$ such that $AS'\perp S'I_A$, and let $AS'\cap BC=Y$. Then $YI_A\perp IA$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point13}
Using the notation of @lem-2point12 and @cor-2point9, $SS'\parallel BC$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $D$ and $T$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $I$ and $I_A$ to $BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of the lower arc $BC$.

By @lem-2point10 and @cor-2point7, the triples $(M,D,S)$ and $(M,T,S')$ are collinear. The result then follows from @lem-2point3 and symmetry across the perpendicular bisector of $BC$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The reflection of $I$ across $O$ is $X(40)$ (the **Bevan point**).
:::

::: {#lem-2point14}
$X(40)$ is the circumcenter of $\triangle I_AI_BI_C$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
By @lem-1point3, the midpoints of $II_A, II_B, II_C$ lie on $(ABC)$.

Applying a homothety centered at $I$ with ratio $2$ shows that $(I_AI_BI_C)$ is the image of $(ABC)$ under this homothety.

Hence the circumcenter of $(I_AI_BI_C)$ is the image of $O$ under the homothety centered at $I$ with ratio $2$, which is $X(40)$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point15}
The midpoint of $H$ and $X(40)$ is $Sp$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
The complements of $I$ and $H$ are $Sp$ and $O$, respectively, so $IH\parallel SpO$.

Moreover, the directed length of $IH$ is $-2$ times that of $SpO$, meaning $IH$ has twice the directed length of $OSp$.

Therefore, the reflection of $I$ across $O$ and the reflection of $H$ across $Sp$ coincide at the same point $X(40)$.
:::

::: {#cor-2point10}
The centroid of $\triangle IHX(40)$ is $G$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
The reflection of $H$ across $O$ is $X(20)$ (the **de Longchamps point**).
:::

::: {#cor-2point11}
The complement of $X(20)$ is $H$.
:::

::: {#lem-2point16}
The midpoint of $Na$ and $X(20)$ is $X(40)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider $\triangle GIO$. Since $X(40)$ is the reflection of $I$ across $O$, it lies on $IO$ with $\dfrac{IX(40)}{X(40)O}=-2$.

Because $X(20)$ is the anticomplement of $H$ (and $H$ is the anticomplement of $O$), $X(20)$ lies on $OG$ with $\dfrac{OX(20)}{X(20)G}=-\dfrac{3}{4}$.

By @lem-2point7, $Na$ lies on $GI$ with $\dfrac{GNa}{NaI}=-\dfrac{2}{3}$.

By @thm-2point1, $X(40), X(20), Na$ are collinear.

Applying @thm-2point1 to $\triangle X(20)NaG$ with transversal $I-X(40)-O$ gives
$$
-1=\frac{NaI}{IG}\times \frac{GO}{OX(20)}\times \frac{X(20)X(40)}{X(40)Na}=-3\times \frac{1}{3}\times \frac{X(20)X(40)}{X(40)Na},
$$
so $X(40)$ is the midpoint of $Na$ and $X(20)$.
:::
